provenance.note: Figures were gathered with WebSearch because WebFetch was blocked in the authoring session; every entry keeps the source URLs it was read from. This is a curated snapshot of public sources, not an authoritative database, and it is baked into the build — the app never fetches anything at runtime.
rules: A null field means the figure is not known or sources disagree irreconcilably. Omit the row — never substitute 0, "unknown", or a guess.
maxLenM is not always a length: read `measure`/`measureLabel` and label it with those words.
group:true entries name a group, not a species; show `groupLine` so the referent is explicit.
habitat freshwater/diadromous entries must say so rather than implying a marine depth.
Band figures (minM/maxM/preferM) are placement heuristics derived from the sourced ranges — they are not themselves sourced figures and must not be displayed as data.
The dot-creature is a procedural rendering, never a depiction of the real animal.

steps: band = the sourced "usually" range when one is quoted (usualMinM/usualMaxM), otherwise the shallow third of the sourced range, because published maxima are records rather than homes.
a band capped by an explicit caveat in the entry (bandCapM) is capped there, with the quote in bandCapNote.
preferM = sqrt(max(minM, maxM/20) * maxM) — the shallow-weighted centre of the band. Depth distributions are heavy at the shallow end.
a band narrower than min(max(0.6*preferM, 4), 60) m is widened up to that, never past the sourced extent, so a school still spreads.
maxima are clamped to 1190 m so nothing is placed inside the seabed.
motion (tight/hold/wander/note) is carried over from the v3.4 authored band; wanderM is rescaled to 12% of the new span.

habitats.diadromous: diadromous — moves between fresh water and the sea

whale.fact: Its heart weighs ~180 kg and its calls reach 188 decibels.
whale.precision: Surface-breather; depth is dive range, not habitat. Foraging dives average ~140 m; deepest tagged dive ~316 m (Croll et al. 2001). Popular sources claiming 500 m are unsupported by tag data. Max length disputed: NOAA states 'about 110 ft' (~33.5 m) but the longest reliably measured specimen is 29.9 m, so 30 m is the defensible figure.

humpback.usualNote: 88.5% of 7,986 tagged dives were shallower than 80 m
humpback.fact: Males sing 20-minute songs, and every male in a region sings the same one.
humpback.precision: Surface-breather. In a South Pacific tagging study of 7,986 dives, 88.5% were shallower than 80 m; deepest recorded dive 616 m. Max length: longest recorded 17.4 m (male) and 18.6 m (female); 18.5 m used as an honest round figure. IUCN downlisted to Least Concern in the Nov 2018 cetacean update (several subpopulations remain EN/CR).

orca.fact: One of the few mammals that goes through menopause; females can pass 90 years.
orca.precision: Surface-breather. Deepest recorded dive 480 m, from Eastern North Pacific offshore killer whales; most foraging is far shallower and depth use varies hugely between ecotypes (resident/transient/offshore). Max length ~10 m for males, ~8.5 m for females. IUCN is Data Deficient specifically because the unresolved species/ecotype split blocks a global assessment.

beluga.fact: A tagged male dived to 956 m in the Canada Basin, under Arctic winter ice.
beluga.precision: Surface-breather. Maximum depth disputed and strongly population-dependent: 350 m in an early free-ranging study, 647 m (SeaWorld), 872 m often cited, and 956 m for a male in the Canada Basin (2016 study). 950 m used as a rounded upper bound; typical dives are far shallower. Deepest-diving stocks are Cumberland Sound, Somerset Island and West Greenland animals wintering over steep basins.

dolphin.usualNote: coastal populations typically dive only 3–46 m
dolphin.fact: Offshore ones dive to 1,000 m; coastal ones rarely go past 50 m.
dolphin.precision: Surface-breather. Depth range varies enormously by ecotype — this is the clearest case in the set. Coastal populations typically dive only 3-46 m; offshore Bermuda animals tagged by Fahlman et al. (2023) reached 1,000 m and 13.8 min. The old 300 m figure is from 'Tuffy', a US Navy-trained dolphin (1965), and badly understates wild capability.

narwhal.fact: Its 3 m tusk is a tooth wired with about 10 million nerve endings.
narwhal.precision: Surface-breather. Tag data show regular dives to 800-1,200 m with maxima exceeding 1,800 m. Max length is body length excluding the tusk (3.6-6.2 m; males average ~4.7 m). IUCN was Near Threatened 2008-2017, downlisted to Least Concern in the 2017 cetacean update — older sources still say NT.

porpoise.fact: Greenland porpoises dive past 400 m, far deeper than their North Sea kin.
porpoise.precision: Surface-breather. Depth varies strongly by population: North Sea animals max around 226 m, while West Greenland porpoises averaged 248 m maximum dive depth with a deepest of 410 m. Global IUCN is Least Concern, but the Baltic Proper and Black Sea subpopulations are separately assessed as far more threatened.

shark.fact: A tagged female named Nicole swam 11,100 km to Australia in 99 days.
shark.precision: FishBase gives depth 0-1280 m, usually 0-250 m; the deep end comes from tagged offshore excursions, not routine habitat. Max length 640 cm TL per FishBase; larger claims (7 m+) are historically unverified.

tuna.fact: Warm-blooded: it holds its core up to 20 C above the surrounding water.
tuna.precision: FishBase depth 0-985 m, usually 0-100 m. Max length 458 cm TL. IUCN moved this species from Endangered to Least Concern in the September 2021 Red List update after quota enforcement worked — many secondary sources (including FishBase text) still say Endangered.

marlin.fact: Adult females can outweigh the biggest males by roughly four times.
marlin.precision: FishBase depth range 0-1000 m for M. nigricans; no 'usually' band is published for this species (the 0-200 m figure often quoted belongs to the Indo-Pacific M. mazara). Max length 500 cm TL. Heaviest recorded female 748 kg vs 170 kg for the largest male. IUCN Vulnerable under criterion A2 (33-37% decline over 27 years).

swordfish.fact: Heater cells warm its eyes and brain 10-15 C above the surrounding sea.
swordfish.precision: FishBase depth 0-2878 m, usually 0-550 m; it makes large daily vertical migrations, which is what the heater organ protects against. Max length 455 cm FL (fork length, not total). Global IUCN assessment is old (2007/2011-era) and Near Threatened.

barracuda.fact: Large ones often carry ciguatoxin, which cooking cannot destroy.
barracuda.precision: FishBase depth 0-100 m, usually 3-30 m — much shallower than its reputation suggests. Max length 200 cm, max weight 50 kg. Widely quoted burst-speed figures (27-36 mph) conflict badly across sources and are deliberately excluded here.

sturgeon.fact: The oldest one recorded was 118 years old; a record fish weighed 1,571 kg.
sturgeon.precision: Beluga sturgeon used as the referent (largest sturgeon). FishBase depth 70-180 m in the sea, wintering to about 100 m; it is anadromous and runs far up rivers to spawn, so the marine band understates where it actually goes. Max length 800 cm TL per FishBase; largest well-documented specimen 720 cm / 1,571 kg.

sunfish.fact: The 2,744 kg heaviest-bony-fish record belongs to its cousin Mola alexandrini.
sunfish.precision: FishBase depth 30-1515 m, usually 30-70 m; it basks at the surface between deep foraging dives, so the shallow minimum of 30 m is a FishBase convention rather than a hard floor. Max length 333 cm TL, max published weight ~1.3 t. The famous 2,300 kg Kamogawa specimen was reidentified in 2022 as M. alexandrini, not M. mola.

oarfish.fact: Submersible footage shows it swimming vertically, head pointed at the surface.
oarfish.precision: FishBase depth 20-1000 m, usually 20-200 m. Max length: reliable records to 8 m; the widely repeated 11 m / 272 kg figure is a historical report and not verified, so 8 m is used. IUCN set to null — no global Red List assessment found for this species.

seahorse.fact: Males get pregnant, feeding embryos through a placenta-like brood pouch.
seahorse.precision: Spotted/common seahorse used as the referent for the generic lexicon word. FishBase depth 0-68 m, usually 0-8 m. Max length 30 cm TL. IUCN Vulnerable, assessed 2012.

moray.fact: A second set of jaws launches from its throat to drag prey down.
moray.precision: Giant moray used as the referent (largest Indo-Pacific moray). FishBase depth 0-50 m, max length 300 cm TL. The pharyngeal-jaw mechanism is from Mehta & Wainwright, Nature 449:79-82 (2007) and is a moray-family trait, not unique to this species.

lamprey.fact: One lamprey can kill up to 18 kg of fish during its parasitic phase.
lamprey.precision: FishBase gives an extraordinary depth range of 1-4099 m; the deep records come from lampreys attached to deep-caught host fish rather than free-living lampreys, so treat the maximum as host-mediated. Max length ~120 cm. Anadromous: spawns in fresh water, feeds at sea.
lamprey.bandCapNote: the deep records come from lampreys attached to deep-caught host fish rather than free-living lampreys

clownfish.fact: All are born male; the biggest fish in the anemone turns female when the queen dies.
clownfish.precision: FishBase: depth 1-15 m (usually 3-15 m), max 11.0 cm TL.

angelfish.measureNote: standard length — total length is slightly greater
angelfish.fact: Juveniles wear blue-white bullseye rings; scientists once called them a separate species.
angelfish.precision: FishBase: 1-100 m, max 40.0 cm SL (standard length, so total length is slightly greater).

lionfish.fact: In the invaded Caribbean, one female can release over 2 million eggs a year.
lionfish.precision: FishBase native-range depth 2-55 m; in the invaded W Atlantic recorded to 304 m off Bermuda. Max 38 cm (43 cm reported in invaded range).

pufferfish.fact: Its tetrodotoxin is roughly 1,200 times deadlier than cyanide, with no antidote.
pufferfish.precision: "Pufferfish" is a family-level name; figures here are for the white-spotted puffer Arothron hispidus (FishBase: 1-50 m, 50 cm TL).

anglerfish.fact: Males are 2-3 cm, fuse to the female's body, and share her bloodstream for life.
anglerfish.precision: Depth 100-4500 m, usually 100-1500 m. Max length is the female (18.0 cm TL); males reach only 1.5-2.8 cm.

salmon.fact: The longest ever netted, in Norway in 1925, measured 160.65 cm.
salmon.precision: FishBase: 0-210 m (usually 10-23 m), max 150 cm; the 160.65 cm Norwegian record is the longest documented individual. Anadromous - spawns in fresh water, matures at sea.

cod.fact: A single large female can release up to 9 million eggs in one spawning.
cod.precision: FishBase: 0-600 m, usually 150-200 m; record 200 cm TL / ~96 kg.

herring.fact: They talk by farting: high-pitched anal gas pulses predators can't hear.
herring.precision: FishBase: 0-364 m, usually 0-200 m; max 45 cm.

mackerel.fact: No swim bladder at all, so it must keep swimming or sink.
mackerel.precision: FishBase: 0-1000 m, usually 0-200 m; max 60.0 cm FL (fork length).

sardine.fact: Schools sink to 100 m by day and rise to 10-35 m to feed at night.
sardine.precision: FishBase: 10-100 m (usually 25-100 m), max 27.5 cm SL.

piranha.fact: Shoaling is defence, not frenzy: lone piranhas breathe faster from fear.
piranha.precision: Depth nulled - FishBase lists no depth range for this Amazon-basin freshwater species and no sourced figure was found. Max 50 cm SL (rarely over 35 cm). No IUCN global assessment located.

grouper.fact: Booms at about 60 Hz with its swim bladder; divers feel the thump.
grouper.precision: FishBase: 0-100 m, usually 0-46 m; max 250 cm (dominant males), ~400 kg. IUCN VU (A2bcd, 2021 assessment).

snapper.fact: Otolith dating has confirmed individuals up to 57-60 years old.
snapper.precision: FishBase: 10-190 m, usually 30-130 m; max 100 cm TL. IUCN VU A2bd (2015 assessment).

trout.fact: Steelhead are the same species: rainbow trout that went to sea.
trout.precision: Flagged freshwater per brief, but O. mykiss also has an anadromous sea-run form (steelhead); FishBase lists it as freshwater/brackish/marine. Depth 0-200 m, max 122 cm TL (sea-run individuals).

bass.fact: Slow-grower: up to 30 years old, and 7 years just to reach legal size.
bass.precision: FishBase: 10-100 m, max 103 cm TL. IUCN category disputed across sources - Near Threatened per FishBase and a 2024 global reassessment, Least Concern in older assessments.

catfish.fact: Some beach themselves to snatch pigeons, succeeding about 28% of the time.
catfish.precision: Max length disputed: 2.73 m / 130 kg is the largest with hard evidence; the widely repeated 5 m / 306 kg figures trace to misidentifications and unit errors. Depth 0-30 m; occasionally enters brackish Baltic/Black Sea water.

wrasse.fact: It scraped a mark it could only see in a mirror - a first for fish.
wrasse.precision: FishBase: 0-100 m, usually 1-30 m; max 14.0 cm TL. The mirror-mark result is real but its interpretation as self-awareness is contested.

koi.fact: Koi are colour morphs of the Amur carp, bred ornamentally since the 1820s.
koi.precision: Both depth and max length nulled. No depth range published for this species. Length figures conflict badly and irreconcilably: FishBase gives 28.0 cm SL for wild Amur carp, while ~90-100 cm is widely claimed for ornamental koi but only in non-scientific hobbyist sources.

goldfish.fact: The 3-second memory is a myth; trained goldfish recall tasks months later.
goldfish.precision: FishBase: 0-20 m, max 48.0 cm TL (occasional reports to 59 cm). Freshwater/brackish. IUCN LC, assessed 2010.

minnow.fact: Its crushed skin releases 'Schreckstoff', the alarm pheromone found in 1938.
minnow.precision: Depth nulled - no published depth range found for this small stream species. Max 14 cm TL (typically ~7 cm). IUCN LC, assessed January 2024.

guppy.fact: Under new predators, wild guppies evolve measurably in as few as 8 generations.
guppy.precision: Depth nulled - FishBase publishes no depth range. Max length is the female (~5 cm); males ~3.5 cm. IUCN category not confirmed by any source consulted.

betta.fact: A labyrinth organ lets it gulp air; fry ride in the male's bubble nest.
betta.precision: Depth nulled - no published range; wild habitat is shallow rice paddies and stagnant pools. Max 6.5 cm TL. IUCN VU in the wild (habitat loss and pollution), despite being ubiquitous in the aquarium trade.

tetra.fact: Its blue stripe is tilting guanine crystals - it dims to indigo in the dark.
tetra.precision: Depth nulled - no published range; native to blackwater tributaries of the Solimoes. Length is FishBase's 2.5 cm SL; ~4 cm TL is commonly reported elsewhere. No IUCN assessment located.

perch.fact: Lays eggs in white lace ribbons up to a metre long, unique to Perca.
perch.precision: FishBase: 1-30 m, usually 3-4 m; max 60.0 cm SL; maximum recorded age 22 years.

pike.fact: Strikes from a standstill at up to 130 m/s2 acceleration.
pike.precision: FishBase: 0-30 m, usually 1-5 m; max 150 cm TL (female), 137 cm FL (male). IUCN LC, assessed 2022. Acceleration measured on ~0.38 m fish.

carp.fact: IUCN Vulnerable in its native range while ranking among the worst invaders.
carp.precision: FishBase: 0-29 m, max 110 cm SL. Freshwater/brackish, benthopelagic.

manta.fact: Highest brain-to-body ratio of any fish; may pass mirror self-recognition.
manta.precision: Size is DISC WIDTH, not body length: 700 cm max (7.1 m measured in one case). Depth 0-1000 m. Uplisted to Endangered in December 2020; some sources still cite the older Vulnerable listing.

stingray.fact: The serrated venomous barb regrows like a fingernail in 3-4 months.
stingray.precision: Size is DISC WIDTH: FishBase 200 cm WD, though 150 cm WD is cited elsewhere. FishBase depth 0-53 m; other sources report the species to 100 m.

skate.fact: At 2.85 m it's the largest skate in European seas - and Critically Endangered.
skate.precision: "Common skate" was split into two species (D. batis and D. intermedius); the 285 cm figure was recorded for the historical D. batis complex, so it may partly reflect flapper skate.

flounder.fact: Born with an eye on each side; one migrates over the skull as it flattens.
flounder.precision: FishBase: 1-100 m, max 60.0 cm TL. Regularly enters estuaries and fresh water.

halibut.fact: World's largest flatfish: 4.7 m, 320 kg, and up to 50 years old.
halibut.precision: IUCN nulled - sources give three different categories (Endangered from the outdated 1996 assessment, Near Threatened, and Vulnerable), so no category is well-established. Depth 50-2000 m, max 470 cm TL.

sole.fact: Lies buried in sand by day with only eyes and nostrils showing.
sole.precision: FishBase: 0-150 m, usually 10-60 m; max 70.0 cm SL. IUCN Data Deficient.

eel.fact: Swims ~5,000 km to the Sargasso Sea; its eyes swell up to 10x first.
eel.precision: FishBase: 0-700 m; max 150 cm (exceptional - normally 60-80 cm). Catadromous: grows in fresh water, spawns in the Atlantic. IUCN CR, assessed 2018.

seasnake.fact: Can't drink seawater - it waits months for rain to form a freshwater lens.
seasnake.precision: Approximate. This is a surface-pelagic snake; the depth figure is measured maximum dive depth (6.8 m dry season, 15.1 m wet season), not a habitat range. Max length ~1.2 m; adults commonly 50-90 cm.

pipefish.fact: The male gets pregnant, brooding eggs in a pouch of two skin folds.
pipefish.precision: FishBase: 0-110 m, usually 3-15 m; max 50.0 cm TL. IUCN LC per Wikipedia; one aggregator lists no assessment.

ribbonfish.fact: A 3 m ribbon that swims vertically, head up, in 300-600 m of water.
ribbonfish.precision: FishBase: bathypelagic, 300-600 m, max 300 cm TL. Looks like an oarfish but is not closely related.

jellyfish.usualNote: other sources give 0–90 m because the animal is almost always near the surface
jellyfish.fact: Moon jellies drift near the surface but have been recorded down to about 1,250 m.
jellyfish.precision: maxLenM is bell diameter: usually ~25 cm, commonly cited max 40 cm (some sources say 50 cm). SeaLifeBase gives depth 0-1250 m; other sources give 0-90 m because the animal is almost always near the surface. IUCN: not evaluated (NE).

manowar.measureNote: disputed: commonly 10–20 m extended; the float itself is ~0.3 m
manowar.fact: Not a jellyfish but a floating colony of four kinds of specialised zooids.
manowar.precision: Obligate surface floater, so depth is 0 m; the float itself is ~0.3 m and rises ~15 cm above the waterline. maxLenM is tentacle length, which is disputed: commonly 10-20 m extended, reported to 30 m and claimed to 50 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

seaangel.measureNote: northern subspecies; the southern one is only ~1.2 cm
seaangel.fact: A shell-less swimming sea slug; the northern form reaches 8.5 cm, largest of any sea angel.
seaangel.precision: Northern subspecies 7-8.5 cm; southern subspecies only ~1.2 cm. Depth given variously as surface to >500 m and 0-600 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

comb.commonName: comb jelly (warty comb jelly / sea walnut)
comb.groupNote: "Comb jelly" is the whole phylum Ctenophora (~200 described species). Referent chosen: Mnemiopsis leidyi.
comb.groupTaxon: "Comb jelly" is the whole phylum Ctenophora (~200 described species).
comb.fact: Its eight comb rows of fused cilia scatter light into rainbows - diffraction, not bioluminescence.
comb.precision: SeaLifeBase max length 18 cm; other sources give 7-12 cm as typical. Depth 5-200 m (pelagic) per SeaLifeBase. Ctenophores are the largest animals that swim using cilia. IUCN: not evaluated.

octopus.fact: Reaches about 1.3 m in total length with a mantle of roughly 25 cm.
octopus.precision: maxLenM is total length (arms included): males to 1.3 m, females to 1.2 m. Mantle length ~0.25 m. Depth 0-200 m.

squid.measureNote: to the tentacle tips; mantle alone ~2 m
squid.fact: Has the largest eyes of any invertebrate and is known mostly from strandings and whale stomachs.
squid.precision: Depth range is poorly known; 300-1,000 m is inferred from trawls and sperm whale dive behaviour. Max total length 12-13 m for females, ~10 m for males, measured to the tentacle tips; claims of 20 m+ are undocumented. Mantle alone ~2 m.

kraken.commonName: kraken (legend; represented by the giant squid)
kraken.groupNote: The kraken is a Scandinavian legendary sea monster, not a taxon. Referent used, per instruction: Architeuthis dux (giant squid).
kraken.groupTaxon: The kraken is a Scandinavian legendary sea monster, not a taxon.
kraken.measureNote: to the tentacle tips; mantle alone ~2 m
kraken.fact: The kraken legend is usually traced to real giant squid, which reach about 13 m.
kraken.precision: All figures are for Architeuthis dux and carry the same caveats as the 'squid' entry. No figure here describes the mythological kraken itself.

cuttlefish.fact: Moves inshore to spawn in spring and summer, wintering at 100-200 m.
cuttlefish.precision: maxLenM is mantle length (49 cm typical maximum; largest recorded individual 60 cm ML). SeaLifeBase depth 0-242 m, usually 0-50 m.

nautilus.fact: Lives on steep reef drop-offs and implodes below roughly 800 m.
nautilus.precision: maxLenM is shell diameter: typically 170-180 mm, up to 222 mm. Depth typically 130-700 m; shell implosion depth commonly quoted as ~2,000 ft (~610 m) to ~800 m, so the deep limit is disputed. IUCN: no nautilus species is currently assessed on the Red List; listed as Threatened under the US ESA (2018) and on CITES Appendix II (2017).

vampyroteuthis.usualNote: typical band 600–1200 m; MBARI found it confined to 600–900 m in Monterey Bay
vampyroteuthis.fact: Lives in the oxygen minimum zone, where oxygen falls to about 0.4 ml per litre.
vampyroteuthis.precision: Meso- to bathypelagic 300-3,000 m; typical band 600-1,200 m, and MBARI work in Monterey Bay found it confined to 600-900 m. Max total length reported as 28-30 cm; mantle length usually 7.9-12.1 cm. IUCN: not evaluated.

starfish.groupNote: "Starfish" is the class Asteroidea (~1,900 species). Referent chosen: Asterias rubens, the common sea star of the North Atlantic.
starfish.groupReferent: Asterias rubens, the common sea star of the North Atlantic
starfish.measureNote: arm tip to arm tip; 10–30 cm is normal
starfish.fact: Ranges from the intertidal down to about 650 m and can span 52 cm across.
starfish.precision: maxLenM is arm-tip-to-arm-tip diameter; 52 cm is the recorded maximum, 10-30 cm is normal. Depth 0-650 m, usually 0-400 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

urchin.groupNote: "Sea urchin" is the class Echinoidea (~950 species). Referent chosen: Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the purple sea urchin of the NE Pacific.
urchin.groupTaxon: "Sea urchin" is the class Echinoidea (~950 species).
urchin.groupReferent: Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, the purple sea urchin of the NE Pacific
urchin.measureNote: usually ~50 mm; spines add to overall size
urchin.fact: Grinds pits into rock with its teeth and spines and can strip kelp forests bare.
urchin.precision: maxLenM is test (shell) diameter: usually ~50 mm, occasionally 100 mm; spines add to overall size. Depth mid-to-low intertidal down to 160 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

crab.groupNote: "Crab" is the infraorder Brachyura plus other decapods (~7,000 species). Referent chosen: Callinectes sapidus, the Atlantic blue crab.
crab.groupTaxon: "Crab" is the infraorder Brachyura plus other decapods (~7,000 species).
crab.groupReferent: Callinectes sapidus, the Atlantic blue crab
crab.measureNote: carapace length is roughly half that
crab.fact: An estuarine swimming crab found from the shoreline down to about 90 m.
crab.precision: maxLenM is carapace WIDTH (up to 23 cm), the standard measurement for this species; carapace length is roughly half that. Depth 0-90 m, usually 0-35 m. IUCN status not confirmed in any source found, so left null.

sanddollar.groupNote: "Sand dollar" is the order Clypeasteroida. Referent chosen: Echinarachnius parma, the common sand dollar of the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
sanddollar.groupReferent: Echinarachnius parma, the common sand dollar of the North Atlantic and North Pacific
sanddollar.fact: A flattened burrowing urchin recorded from the low tide line down to about 1,500 m.
sanddollar.precision: maxLenM is test diameter, 5-10 cm when fully grown. The 1,500 m (5,000 ft) figure is an occasional extreme; the species is normally shallow subtidal. IUCN: not evaluated.
sanddollar.bandCapNote: the 1,500 m figure is an occasional extreme; the species is normally shallow subtidal

basketstar.groupNote: "Basket star" is the family Gorgonocephalidae. Referent chosen: Gorgonocephalus arcticus, the northern basket star.
basketstar.groupReferent: Gorgonocephalus arcticus, the northern basket star
basketstar.measureNote: other Gorgonocephalus species unfurl to ~1.2 m
basketstar.fact: A brittle star whose arms branch repeatedly into a filter-feeding basket.
basketstar.precision: maxLenM is total diameter, up to ~400 mm for this species; other Gorgonocephalus species unfurl to ~1.2 m. Depth low intertidal / sublittoral down to 1,500 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

brittlestar.groupNote: "Brittle star" is the class Ophiuroidea (~2,000+ species). Referent chosen: Ophiothrix fragilis, the common brittle star of NE Atlantic waters.
brittlestar.groupTaxon: "Brittle star" is the class Ophiuroidea (~2,000+ species).
brittlestar.groupReferent: Ophiothrix fragilis, the common brittle star of NE Atlantic waters
brittlestar.measureNote: one arm; full span is roughly 20 cm
brittlestar.fact: Forms dense beds where thousands of arms sieve food from the current.
brittlestar.precision: maxLenM is single arm length (~10 cm); the central disc is up to 2 cm across and arms are about five times the disc diameter, so full span is roughly 20 cm. Depth: shallow to 350 m (some sources say 200 m). IUCN: not evaluated.

anemone.groupNote: "Sea anemone" is the order Actiniaria (~1,100 species). Referent chosen: Actinia equina, the beadlet anemone.
anemone.groupTaxon: "Sea anemone" is the order Actiniaria (~1,100 species).
anemone.fact: Survives hours of air exposure at low tide by pulling its tentacles into a jelly blob.
anemone.precision: maxLenM is diameter when expanded (under 10 cm); height 6-8 cm, basal disc up to 5 cm. Mainly intertidal, rarely subtidal to ~20 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

coral.groupNote: "Reef-building coral" spans hundreds of scleractinian species. Referent chosen: Acropora cervicornis, Caribbean staghorn coral.
coral.groupTaxon: "Reef-building coral" spans hundreds of scleractinian species.
coral.usualNote: the typical depth band on forereefs is 5–25 m
coral.fact: One of the fastest-growing corals, adding up to about 20 cm of branch a year.
coral.precision: maxLenM is branch length (a few cm to over 2 m). Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List since 2008; population declined at least 80% over 30 years and is now under 3% of former abundance. Typical depth band on forereefs is 5-25 m.

kelp.usualNote: anchors on rock mostly at 6–30 m and needs bottom light above 1% of surface
kelp.measureNote: holdfast to canopy; reports up to 60 m
kelp.fact: Among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth, adding up to 50 cm a day.
kelp.precision: maxLenM is frond height from holdfast to canopy: commonly 30-45 m, with reports up to 60 m. Anchors on rock mostly at 6-30 m and needs bottom light above 1% of surface, so it rarely exceeds ~40 m. IUCN: no Red List assessment found.

seagrass.groupNote: "Seagrass" covers ~72 species of marine flowering plants. Referent chosen: Thalassia testudinum, Caribbean turtlegrass.
seagrass.groupTaxon: "Seagrass" covers ~72 species of marine flowering plants.
seagrass.usualNote: to 30 m where water is clear, typically 0–10 m
seagrass.fact: A true flowering plant, not an alga, forming meadows down to about 30 m in clear water.
seagrass.precision: maxLenM is blade length, reported as up to 30 cm in some sources and 10-60 cm in others. Depth to 30 m where water is clear, typically 0-10 m. IUCN Least Concern (2010 global assessment); a 2025 Tropical Atlantic regional assessment raised it to Near Threatened, so the status is in flux.

seaweed.groupNote: "Seaweed" is an informal term for thousands of marine macroalgae. Referent chosen: Fucus vesiculosus, bladderwrack.
seaweed.groupTaxon: "Seaweed" is an informal term for thousands of marine macroalgae.
seaweed.fact: Paired gas bladders lift its fronds toward the light as the tide comes in.
seaweed.precision: depthMaxM is null on purpose: MarLIN states depth is not a meaningful variable because the species is intertidal, occurring only at shallow depths in the low-salinity Baltic. Length usually 20-60 cm, growing to 150 cm and recorded to 2 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

sargassum.groupNote: Sargassum is a genus of ~350 species; the floating Atlantic mats are mainly S. natans and S. fluitans. Referent chosen: Sargassum natans.
sargassum.groupTaxon: Sargassum is a genus of ~350 species; the floating Atlantic mats are mainly S. natans and S. fluitans.
sargassum.fact: In June 2018 the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt ran 8,850 km and held over 20 million tonnes.
sargassum.precision: Holopelagic: it never attaches to the seafloor and lives at the surface, hence depth 0 m. maxLenM is frond length (roughly 10-200 cm); mats themselves stretch far further. IUCN: not evaluated.
sargassum.surfaceFloater: holopelagic — it never attaches to the seafloor

wakame.fact: One of the world's most invasive seaweeds, now on every continent except Africa and Antarctica.
wakame.precision: Fronds usually reach 1.5 m and have been recorded to 3 m; growth up to 1 cm/day. Depth low intertidal to 18 m (some sources say 15-20 m), with most biomass at 1-3 m. IUCN: not Red List assessed, but listed in the IUCN Global Invasive Species Database.

eelgrass.usualNote: MarLIN: typically down to 4 m in sheltered UK waters
eelgrass.fact: Meadows of it store carbon and shelter juvenile fish in sheltered bays and estuaries.
eelgrass.precision: Depth is light-limited and highly site-specific: MarLIN gives 'typically down to 4 m' in sheltered UK waters, and a Kiel Bight (Baltic) study records 0.6-7.6 m, which is the figure used here. It is not a global maximum. Leaves usually 20-50 cm, up to 2 m.

seafan.groupNote: "Sea fan" / gorgonian covers hundreds of octocoral species. Referent chosen: Gorgonia ventalina, the Caribbean common sea fan.
seafan.groupTaxon: "Sea fan" / gorgonian covers hundreds of octocoral species.
seafan.groupReferent: Gorgonia ventalina, the Caribbean common sea fan
seafan.measureNote: colony height; up to 150 cm wide
seafan.fact: Grows as a flat mesh oriented across the prevailing current to strain out plankton.
seafan.precision: maxLenM is colony height, up to 180 cm tall and 150 cm wide. Depth roughly 1-30 m (3-100 ft); most common shallower than ~15 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

plankton.groupNote: "Phytoplankton" is a functional group of thousands of species (diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, cyanobacteria). Referent chosen: Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, formerly Emiliania huxleyi.
plankton.groupTaxon: "Phytoplankton" is a functional group of thousands of species (diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, cyanobacteria).
plankton.usualNote: the euphotic zone, ~0–200 m in clear water
plankton.fact: Its chalk-plated blooms cover over 100,000 square kilometres and are visible from space.
plankton.precision: maxLenM is cell diameter, about 5 micrometres = 5e-6 m. Phytoplankton span <1 to >100 micrometres. Depth is the euphotic zone, ~0-200 m in clear water. NOAA credits the ocean, chiefly phytoplankton, with roughly half of Earth's photosynthetic oxygen production. IUCN: not evaluated (no Red List assessments exist for phytoplankton).

krill.measureNote: disputed: BAS says up to 6 cm, SeaLifeBase records 3.0 cm
krill.fact: One of the most abundant animals on Earth, with biomass estimated near 379 million tonnes.
krill.precision: Length is disputed: the British Antarctic Survey states up to 6 cm, while SeaLifeBase records a maximum of 3.0 cm TL. Depth normally 0-300 m (usually 15-130 m) with adults occasionally to 600 m; BAS has filmed krill feeding down to 3,000 m, so 600 m is a conservative maximum. IUCN Least Concern, assessed 2015.

shrimp.groupNote: "Shrimp" spans thousands of caridean and penaeid species. Referent chosen: Pandalus borealis, the northern or coldwater shrimp.
shrimp.groupTaxon: "Shrimp" spans thousands of caridean and penaeid species.
shrimp.groupReferent: Pandalus borealis, the northern or coldwater shrimp
shrimp.fact: Starts life male and later changes sex to female, a pattern called protandry.
shrimp.precision: maxLenM is female maximum (16.5 cm); males reach 12.0 cm. Depth 9-1,450 m, usually 50-500 m. IUCN: not evaluated.

salp.groupNote: "Salp" is the family Salpidae (~50 species). Referent chosen: Salpa fusiformis, the common salp.
salp.fact: A barrel-shaped tunicate that links into drifting chains and migrates up each night to feed.
salp.precision: maxLenM 5.2 cm for a single zooid; solitary zooids are usually 22-52 mm. Depth 0-800 m with diel vertical migration. IUCN: not evaluated.

algae.groupNote: "Algae" is an informal grouping of many unrelated lineages. Referent chosen: Ulva lactuca, sea lettuce, a green macroalga.
algae.groupTaxon: "Algae" is an informal grouping of many unrelated lineages.
algae.groupReferent: Ulva lactuca, sea lettuce, a green macroalga
algae.fact: Its blade is only two cells thick, which is why it looks like translucent green paper.
algae.precision: SeaLifeBase gives max length 100 cm and depth 0-108 m; most individuals are far smaller (18-30 cm) and blades over 40 cm occur only in sheltered sites. IUCN: not evaluated.

goldfish.note: a pond fish, near the light

swordfish.note: sunlit by night, twilight by day

anglerfish.note: carries its own lure into the dark

dragon.note: the dark half of the column

oarfish.note: a vertical ribbon in the blue

octo.note: works the reef and the shelf

nautilus.note: rises at night, sinks by day

argonaut.note: a paper shell near the surface

brittlestar.note: sieves the current on the shelf floor

krill.note: rises at night, sinks by day

nebula.note: a cloud with nowhere to be

kelp.note: a holdfast in the forest light

sargassum.note: a floating mat at the surface

coral.note: a reef head in the light

zones.name: Epipelagic zone
facts: The only layer with enough light for photosynthesis.
Holds the vast majority of commercial fisheries.
zones.precision: NOAA calls the upper 200 m the euphotic or sunlight zone. The base is conventionally the depth where photosynthetically active radiation falls to 1% of surface value, which is 200-250 m in the clearest ocean water and far shallower in turbid coastal water.

zones.name: Mesopelagic zone
facts: Too dark for photosynthesis, lit mainly by bioluminescence.
Source of the daily vertical migration, Earth's largest animal migration.
zones.precision: 200-1000 m is the standard definition (NOAA, WHOI). WHOI notes recent acoustic estimates put twilight-zone fish biomass around 10 billion tonnes, possibly ten times earlier estimates - that figure is contested and is not used as a headline fact.

zones.name: Bathypelagic zone
facts: No sunlight at all reaches this layer.
Pressure runs from roughly 100 to 400 atmospheres.
zones.precision: Pressure figure follows the standard 1 atm per 10 m of depth. WHOI describes the midnight zone as the single largest habitat on Earth, often quoted as about 70% of all seawater; that share depends on where you set the boundaries, so it is left out of the headline facts.

zones.name: Abyssopelagic zone
facts: Named from the Greek for bottomless.
Water sits near freezing, around 2-3 degrees Celsius.
zones.precision: 4000-6000 m is the standard definition. Below about 4000 m calcium carbonate shells dissolve, leaving a seafloor of brown clay and silica.

temperature.label: Surface
temperature.note: Global average sea surface temperature is about 17 C; the observed range across the world ocean surface is about -2 to 36 C.
temperature.precision: Global mean, not a local reading.

temperature.label: Base of the mixed layer
temperature.note: The wind-mixed surface layer is roughly isothermal to 100-200 m, so 200 m is still near surface temperature; the main thermocline begins here and falls steeply below.
temperature.precision: Set to null deliberately. No source found gives a global mean temperature at exactly 200 m; Britannica describes the thermocline as running from about 200 m to about 1000 m with temperature falling from roughly 20 C at the top to about 2 C at the bottom, but that 20 C is a low-latitude figure and would be badly wrong at high latitudes.

temperature.label: Base of the thermocline
temperature.note: Below the thermocline the ocean is nearly isothermal; sources put this depth at about 2-4 C.
temperature.precision: Sources disagree: Britannica gives about 2 C below the thermocline, while the bathypelagic zone (1000-4000 m) is commonly described as a near-constant 4 C. Point value left null and the disagreement expressed as a range.

temperature.label: Abyssal
temperature.note: Abyssal water sits at about 2-3 C through the great majority of its volume; the global average of 2000 m water is about 2.5 C.
temperature.precision: Point value left null; 2-3 C is the sourced band. For context, the average temperature of all ocean water from surface to seafloor is about 3.5 C.

lightRemaining.note: Only 16% of surface light is still present at 10 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Clear open-ocean water. For reference the same source gives 45% remaining at 1 m, because infrared is absorbed almost immediately.

lightRemaining.note: About 1% of the original light is left at 100 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Clear open-ocean water. The 1% level is the conventional base of the euphotic zone, which is why the euphotic depth can be as shallow as 100 m in some water and 200-250 m in the very clearest.

lightRemaining.note: Under 1% remains; NOAA states there is rarely any significant light beyond 200 m.
lightRemaining.precision: Set to null deliberately. No source found gives a numeric percentage at exactly 200 m. 200 m is the conventional 1%-of-surface euphotic depth in the clearest water, so the true value is at or below 1% and is often far lower.

lightRemaining.note: Effectively zero; 1000 m is the deepest sunlight reaches under the best conditions.
lightRemaining.precision: Set to null deliberately. NOAA: sunlight may travel about 1,000 m into the ocean under the right conditions, but there is rarely any significant light beyond 200 m. Below 1000 m is the aphotic zone, where no sunlight penetrates.
